body.heading: Light in, electrons out
paragraphs: A solar panel turns light directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect. When a particle of light — a photon — with enough energy strikes the panel's silicon, it can knock an electron free from its atom, leaving behind a gap called a hole.

Free electrons alone would just wander and recombine. The panel's trick is a built-in one-way slope: two layers of silicon, treated with different impurities, create an electric field at their junction that sweeps electrons in one direction only — and that directed flow is an electric current.

body.heading: From cell to rooftop
paragraphs: A single cell produces only about half a volt, so panels wire dozens of cells in series to reach useful voltages, and seal them under glass against the weather. The electricity produced is direct current, like a battery's.

Homes run on alternating current, so a box called an inverter converts the panel's DC into AC matched to the house and the grid. Any surplus flows out to the grid; when clouds gather or night falls, the house draws power back.

body.heading: How much sunlight becomes power
paragraphs: A typical modern panel converts around a fifth of the sunlight hitting it into electricity — about 20 percent efficiency. The rest becomes heat or is reflected, and researchers keep nudging the figure up a little each decade.

Even so, the raw resource is vast: sunlight delivers roughly a kilowatt to each sun-facing square metre at noon in clear weather. A modest rooftop array of fifteen or so panels can cover much of an average home's yearly electricity use in a sunny climate. No moving parts, no fuel and no noise are involved at any stage.
